letters.name: dlouhé á
letters.tip: The čárka (´) only makes a vowel longer. It never shows stress. pas and pás are different words.

letters.name: bé
letters.tip: At the end of a word it sounds like p: chléb → [chlép].

letters.name: cé
letters.sound: like the "ts" in "cats", even at the start of a word
letters.tip: Never like the "c" in "cat" or "city".

letters.name: dé
letters.tip: Before i, í and ě it becomes ď: dívka sounds like [ďívka].

letters.name: ďé
letters.sound: like the "d" in British "duty": d and y pronounced together
letters.tip: The capital is written Ď. You'll hear the sound more often than you see the letter, because di, dí and dě are pronounced ďi, ďí, ďe.

letters.name: dlouhé é
letters.sound: long version of e, like "ai" in "fair" (without the r)

letters.name: e s háčkem
letters.sound: an "e" that changes the consonant before it
letters.tip: bě, pě, vě, fě sound like bje, pje, vje, fje (věc → [vjec]); dě, tě, ně sound like ďe, ťe, ňe (děkuju → [ďekuju]); mě sounds like mňe (město → [mňesto]).

letters.name: gé
letters.tip: Never like the "g" in "gym". Mostly in borrowed words.

letters.name: há
letters.sound: a voiced h: like the "h" in "behind", with the voice on
letters.tip: Softer and "buzzier" than English h. At the end of a word it sounds like ch: sníh → [sňích].

letters.name: chá
letters.sound: like the "ch" in Scottish "loch", never like "church"
letters.tip: Ch counts as one letter and comes after h in the dictionary: chata comes after hrad.

letters.name: í
letters.tip: Called "měkké i" (soft i). After d, t, n it softens them: ti sounds like ťi, ni like ňi.

letters.name: jé
letters.tip: Never like English j in "jam".

letters.name: ká
letters.sound: like English k, but without the puff of air

letters.name: el
letters.tip: Can be a syllable on its own, with no vowel: vlk (wolf).

letters.name: eň
letters.tip: Also heard in ni, ní and ně: nic sounds like [ňic].

letters.name: pé
letters.sound: like English p, but without the puff of air

letters.name: er
letters.sound: a tapped or rolled r, made with the tip of the tongue
letters.tip: Can be a syllable on its own: Brno, krk (neck), čtvrtek (Thursday).

letters.name: eř
letters.sound: a sound unique to Czech: a rolled r and the "s" in "measure" at the same time
letters.tip: Try a rolled r with the tongue a little tenser and let it buzz like ž. Even Czech children learn it last. If it won't come yet, say ž: you'll be understood.

letters.name: es
letters.sound: always like the "s" in "see", never like "z"

letters.name: té
letters.sound: like English t, but without the puff of air
letters.tip: Before i, í and ě it becomes ť: ticho sounds like [ťicho].

letters.name: ťé
letters.sound: like the "t" in British "tune": t and y pronounced together
letters.tip: Dobrou chuť! = Enjoy your meal! The capital is written Ť.

letters.name: ú s čárkou
letters.tip: Usually only at the start of a word (úterý) or a word part (neúspěch).

letters.name: ů s kroužkem
letters.sound: exactly the same sound as ú
letters.tip: The kroužek (˚) spelling is used in the middle and at the end of words: dům, domů. It sounds the same as ú.

letters.name: ypsilon
letters.sound: exactly the same sound as i
letters.tip: Called "tvrdé y" (hard y). It sounds like i, but after d, t, n it keeps them hard: dy = [dy], di = [ďi]. Czechs spend years at school learning when to write i or y.

letters.name: dlouhé ý
letters.sound: exactly the same sound as í

practice.title: Sounds to letters
practice.description: Which Czech letter makes this sound? Type the letter. Here the háček or čárka is the whole point, so it has to be exact.

exercises.prompt: Which letter sounds like the **"ch" in "church"**?
exercises.why: č (c with a háček) is the "ch" in "church": čaj, Čech.

hints.explain: In Czech, ch is the sound in Scottish "loch". The "church" sound is č.
Plain c is "ts" as in "cats". Add the háček: č.

exercises.prompt: Which letter sounds like the **"sh" in "ship"**?
exercises.why: š is the "sh" in "ship": škola, šéf.

hints.explain: Plain s is always "s" as in "see". With a háček, š is "sh".

exercises.prompt: Which letter sounds like the **"s" in "measure"**?
exercises.why: ž is the sound in "measure": žena, Žofie.

hints.explain: z is the "z" in "zoo". The "measure" sound is ž.

exercises.prompt: Which letter sounds like the **"ts" in "cats"**?
exercises.why: Czech c is always "ts": cena [tsena], Cyril.

hints.explain: Czech writes this sound with one letter: c.

exercises.prompt: Which letter (two characters) sounds like the **"ch" in Scottish "loch"**?
exercises.why: ch is the "loch" sound: chleba, Chrudim. It counts as one letter.

hints.explain: č is the "church" sound. The "loch" sound is written ch.
Czech h is a voiced, softer h. The "loch" sound is ch.

exercises.prompt: Which letter sounds like the **"y" in "yes"**?
exercises.why: Czech j is the English "y" sound: jo, jídlo.

hints.explain: Czech y is a vowel (it sounds like i). The "yes" sound is j.

exercises.prompt: Which letter sounds like the **"ny" in "canyon"**?
exercises.why: ň is "ny": Plzeň, kůň.

hints.explain: Add the háček: ň.

exercises.prompt: Which letter is the sound in **Dvořák** that English doesn't have?
exercises.why: ř: a rolled r and ž at the same time. Dvořák, řeka.

hints.explain: Plain r is a tapped r. The special sound is ř.
Close: ř sounds like r and ž together, but it's written ř.

exercises.prompt: Which letter has a **kroužek** (a small ring) and sounds like **"oo" in "food"**?
exercises.why: ů sounds exactly like ú. It's written in the middle and at the end of words: dům, domů.

hints.explain: ú is the same sound, but it has a čárka, not a kroužek. The letter with the ring is ů.

exercises.prompt: Which vowel sounds **exactly the same as i**?
exercises.why: y (tvrdé y) sounds exactly like i. The difference is only in spelling, and in how d, t, n before it are pronounced.

hints.explain: í is the long version of i. The other letter that sounds like i is y.

practice.title: Reading rules
practice.description: Czech is read almost exactly as it is written, once you know a handful of rules.

exercises.prompt: Which syllable of a Czech word is stressed? (first, second or last)
exercises.why: Czech stress is always on the first syllable: Olomouc = O-lo-mouc. A čárka shows a long vowel, not stress.

hints.explain: Czech always stresses the first syllable, even in long words.
Czech always stresses the first syllable.

exercises.prompt: Pas and pás are different words. Which one means **"passport"**?
exercises.why: pas (short a) = passport; pás (long á) = belt, waist. Vowel length changes the meaning.

hints.explain: pás, with a long á, means belt or waist. Passport is pas.

exercises.prompt: Byt and být are different words. Which one means **"to be"**?
exercises.why: být (long ý) = to be; byt (short y) = flat, apartment.

hints.explain: byt is "flat, apartment". "To be" has a long ý: být.

exercises.prompt: In **dívka** (girl), is the d pronounced as d or ď?
exercises.why: d before i, í or ě is pronounced ď: dívka [ďívka]. (The same for t → ť and n → ň.)

hints.explain: Before i, í or ě, d is softened to ď: [ďívka].

exercises.prompt: How does the final **d** in **hrad** (castle) sound: d or t?
exercises.why: Consonants at the end of a word lose their voice: hrad sounds like [hrat], chléb like [chlép].

hints.explain: At the end of a word, d is pronounced t: [hrat].

exercises.prompt: How is **město** (town) pronounced? Type it the way it sounds, using ň.
exercises.why: mě is pronounced mňe: město [mňesto], mě [mňe].

hints.explain: The ě changes the m before it: mě sounds like mňe, so [mňesto].
After b, p, v, f, ě sounds like je; after m it sounds like ňe: [mňesto].

exercises.prompt: How many vowels are there in this famous tongue-twister? Type a number.
exercises.why: None. "Strč prst skrz krk" (Stick a finger through your throat) works because r and l can form syllables on their own, as in Brno and vlk.

practice.title: Understanding spelling
practice.description: On the phone or at an office, Czechs spell names and e-mail addresses letter by letter. Type the word being spelled.

exercises.prompt: Type the surname being spelled.
exercises.cs: en – ó – vé – á s čárkou – ká
exercises.why: en – ó – vé – á s čárkou – ká spells Novák.

hints.explain: Listen for "á s čárkou": the a is long. Novák.

exercises.prompt: Type the surname being spelled.
exercises.cs: dé – vé – ó – eř – á s čárkou – ká
exercises.why: dé – vé – ó – eř – á s čárkou – ká spells Dvořák.

hints.explain: "eř" is ř and "á s čárkou" is á: Dvořák.

exercises.prompt: Type the surname being spelled.
exercises.cs: eš – ťé – á – es – té – en – á s čárkou
exercises.why: eš – ťé – á – es – té – en – á s čárkou spells Šťastná.

exercises.prompt: Type the surname being spelled.
exercises.why: ká – ú – chá – á – eř spells Kuchař. Notice "chá" is one letter, ch.

hints.explain: "chá" is the letter ch, not č (čé).
The last letter is "eř": ř.

exercises.prompt: Type the e-mail address being spelled.
exercises.cs: jé, á, en, á, tečka, en, ó, vé, á, ká, ó, vé, á, zavináč, seznam, tečka, cé, zet
exercises.why: jé – á – en – á – tečka – novakova – zavináč – seznam – tečka – cé – zet. "tečka" is a dot and "zavináč" is @. Czech e-mail addresses are usually written without diacritics.

exercises.prompt: Type the name being spelled with the phone alphabet.
exercises.cs: H jako Helena, á s čárkou, J jako Josef, E jako Emil, K jako Karel
exercises.why: H jako Helena, A s čárkou, J jako Josef, E jako Emil, K jako Karel: Hájek. "jako" means "as in".

practice.title: Spelling your own name
practice.description: How do you say these letters and symbols when spelling aloud? Type the Czech name.

exercises.prompt: How do you name the letter **š** when spelling?
exercises.why: š is called "eš". Consonants are named either with -é (bé, cé, dé…) or with e- in front (ef, el, em, en, er, es, eš…).

hints.explain: š is one of the letters named with e- in front: eš.

exercises.prompt: How do you name the letter **w** when spelling?
exercises.why: w is "dvojité vé" (double v). You'll need it for website and e-mail addresses.

hints.explain: Czechs say "dvojité vé" for w.
In Czech: dvojité vé.

exercises.prompt: How do you name the letter **y** when spelling?
exercises.why: y is "ypsilon" or "tvrdé y" (hard y), to distinguish it from i ("měkké i").

hints.explain: That's the name of i. y is ypsilon (or tvrdé y).

exercises.prompt: How do you name the letter **j** when spelling?
exercises.why: j is "jé". Careful: English "jay" would be understood as "dž".

hints.explain: That's the English name. In Czech, j is "jé".

exercises.prompt: How do you name the letter **h** when spelling?
exercises.why: h is "há". (ch is "chá".)

exercises.prompt: What do you call the **@** symbol in an e-mail address?
exercises.why: @ is "zavináč", literally a rolled pickled herring.

hints.explain: Czechs say "zavináč" for @.

exercises.prompt: What do you call the **dot** in an e-mail address?
exercises.why: A dot is "tečka": seznam tečka cé zet = seznam.cz.

exercises.prompt: Say "**D as in David**" the Czech way.
exercises.why: Use "jako" (as/like) with the phone-spelling alphabet: D jako David, Č jako Čeněk.
